I’ll find something I genuinely want to learn, like coding, product management, or a new technical skill, and make a plan to start. The annoying part is that I’m genuinely interested in learning these things, but I often end up spending more time figuring out what to learn, finding the right resources, and planning than actually learning. By the time I have free time, I’m either tired or don’t know where to start, so the cycle repeats.

I was standing in my kitchen at 8 PM after a long shift at the plant, staring at a completely empty pantry. I needed milk for the morning, eggs for breakfast, and a few basic vegetables to throw together a quick dinner. I pulled out my phone and opened my preferred quick-commerce app. The cart I had meticulously built during my lunch break had automatically timed out and cleared itself.

Frustrated, I started rebuilding the list from memory. Just as I finally hit checkout, the screen flashed a High Demand Surge warning, and the delivery estimate violently jumped from 12 minutes to "Tomorrow 8 AM." I had to put my boots back on and walk down to the local kirana store. They were completely out of eggs. I walked to a second shop down the road, which only stocked the absurdly overpriced organic ones. I ended up hauling two heavy, mismatched plastic bags back to my room, sweating through my shirt, having wasted nearly an hour of my evening on a task that was supposed to take three taps on a screen.

The entire time, my brain—which spends all day analyzing process efficiencies and identifying non-value-added activities—was screaming. We have built all this incredible logistics infrastructure, yet personal household inventory remains a completely broken, manual chore badly disguised as modern convenience.
column31:
My current system is a deeply embarrassing clash between my formal training in process optimization and the harsh reality of bachelor survival mode. Theoretically, I run my room's groceries on a strict Kanban system. I literally have a mini whiteboard stuck to my wall with three columns: "Stock Optimal," "Reorder Point," and "Critical." It is a beautiful, textbook application of lean inventory management that completely falls apart the moment I actually have to use it.

The real, roundabout system is a chaotic three-tier escalation process.

Tier 1: The WhatsApp Ghost Town
I have a WhatsApp group titled "Room Inventory" where I am the sole member. Throughout my workday at the plant, whenever I remember I am out of toothpaste or bread, I text it to this group. The fatal flaw is that I never actually open this chat when I am in a position to buy anything. It is purely a digital dumping ground for fleeting thoughts.

Tier 2: The Quick-Commerce Graveyard
By mid-week, when the whiteboard is entirely ignored and the WhatsApp group has fifteen unread messages to myself, I start building carts on Zepto or Swiggy Instamart during my lunch break. But because my schedule is erratic, I hesitate to hit checkout. These carts sit in limbo, timing out, refreshing, and automatically deleting items until I finally give up.

Tier 3: The Kirana Store Walk of Shame
Ultimately, 80% of my household procurement defaults to the local kirana store owner just outside the colony gates. We have an unspoken, high-friction understanding. I walk in at 8:30 PM, looking exhausted, and just start pointing at things. He keeps a mental ledger of my purchases because UPI network drops are a daily feature and I never have exact change. I end up doing a massive, uncoordinated haul of heavy detergent, random biscuit packets, and whatever vegetables look least wilted, completely ignoring the carefully curated lean principles on my wall. It is highly inefficient, completely manual, and the only thing that actually keeps me fed.

I was standing outside a partially rusted rolling shutter in Pantnagar at 5:45 AM, already sweating through my t-shirt, trying to negotiate a short-term gym membership before my plant shift started. Relocating for a two-month summer stint meant my usual university routine was completely dismantled, and I desperately needed a reliable place to train before spending the next ten hours analyzing inbound logistics and trying to eliminate non-value-added activities on the shop floor.

I had tracked down this specific local gym on Google Maps because it was the only one claiming to open before 6 AM. When I walked in, the owner was half-asleep on a plastic chair, sipping tea. I asked for a simple, two-month access plan. He flatly refused, tapping a laminated, handwritten chart on the desk. He only offered a strict six-month lock-in or an exorbitant daily pass rate that made zero financial sense for a student.

What followed was a ridiculously inefficient, high-friction negotiation. I tried explaining my temporary relocation. He countered by offering a "special" three-month package, but mandated that I pay the entire sum upfront in cash—blatantly ignoring the massive UPI QR code taped to the mirror directly behind his head. The scanner "wasn't accepting large amounts today," he casually claimed.

The exact task I had to deal with was not fitness; it was the agonizing administrative friction of just trying to pay someone to let me use their equipment. I had to leave the premises, walk three blocks to a dusty ATM that turned out to be out of service, and then hike another two blocks to find a functioning machine. I finally returned with physical currency, completely mentally drained before I had even touched a single dumbbell.

Our wearable tech tracks our heart rate variability down to the millisecond, yet the physical infrastructure of accessing local wellness spaces remains deeply fragmented, entirely unstructured, and completely hostile to transient schedules.

My current fitness system is a spectacular collision between operational theory and practical laziness. On my laptop, I have a beautifully color-coded Excel tracker structured like a Lean Six Sigma optimization project. It has tabs for macronutrient distribution, progressive overload tracking, and recovery metrics. I haven’t updated a single cell since the first week of my PGDM program.

The actual, functioning system is held together entirely by guilt, algorithmic roulette, and incidental panic-cardio.

The StratX Guilt Trip
My primary accountability mechanism is a WhatsApp group with my old case competition teammates. We don't actually log our workouts or share routines. Instead, the chat serves as a repository for passive-aggressive memes about deteriorating posture and the cardiovascular toll of late-night PPT formatting. Seeing a teammate post a picture of a 6 AM run is usually the only thing that shames me into doing push-ups before a morning lecture at FORE.

Incidental Shop-Floor Cardio
During my recent summer stint at the plant in Pantnagar, I completely abandoned the idea of a structured gym routine after that disastrous negotiation with the local owner. My entire cardiovascular baseline was instead sustained by power-walking across massive industrial sheds. I would justify skipping leg day because I had just spent four hours dodging forklifts and pacing the inbound logistics bays while mapping out activities for my MOST implementation project. If I was sweating and my step count was over 15,000, I mentally logged it as a workout.

YouTube Roulette
When I am back in my room and actually decide to train, I outsource all decision-making to the YouTube algorithm. I refuse to use dedicated fitness apps because the paywalls, subscription models, and notification spam drive me crazy. Instead, I just type "15-minute brutal HIIT" into the search bar, click on the first thumbnail with someone looking exhausted, and let autoplay dictate my suffering. I never save the videos, meaning every workout is a completely randomized, unstructured surprise.

I was standing outside a chaotic railway station exit at 11:30 PM, designated as the unofficial "inbound logistics coordinator" for my cousin's wedding. My exact task was supposedly simple: coordinate the pickup of forty-five extended family members arriving on three different delayed trains and route them to two separate guesthouses using four hired tempo travellers.

Instead, I found myself in the middle of a completely unstructured operational nightmare. One driver had gone rogue, parking at the wrong exit and refusing to answer his phone. Two trains that were supposed to be staggered by an hour arrived simultaneously. Meanwhile, the dedicated "Travel Updates" WhatsApp group was entirely useless, clogged with irrelevant emojis and panicked voice notes from an uncle who couldn't find his luggage.

My brain, steeped in process optimization and eliminating non-value-added activities on industrial shop floors, was practically short-circuiting. There was absolutely zero process standardization. I was literally leaning against a tea stall, sketching a makeshift routing sequence on the back of a wedding invitation envelope. I found myself mentally trying to apply predetermined motion time systems to calculate exactly how long it would take a group of exhausted aunties to board a bus with oversized suitcases.

For two hours, I sprinted between platforms and parking lots, manually cross-checking a disorganized spreadsheet on a phone screen that kept freezing in the cold. Every time I fixed one bottleneck, another appeared. The driver who was supposed to go to the first guesthouse ended up taking half the guests to the second one because someone’s grandfather confidently gave him the wrong directions.

We treat Indian wedding logistics like a natural disaster that simply requires brute human force, endless phone calls, and shouting to resolve. It is a completely broken, manual chore disguised as family bonding, and the sheer volume of friction makes it impossible to actually enjoy the celebration.
column46:
My current system for managing weddings is a completely decentralized, high-friction reliance on shadow hierarchies and burner spreadsheets. I try to apply strict supply chain principles to family gatherings, and the structure instantly collapses.

The Shadow Hierarchy
Despite my background in analyzing operations and unit planning, my actual crisis-management system is just delegating the most critical bottlenecks to "Vendor Uncle." Every Indian family has one. I treat him like a chaotic Third-Party Administrator. When the inbound logistics fail—like the hired tempo traveller going rogue—I bypass all logical problem-solving and just call him. He operates entirely on implicit authority, oral contracts, and aggressive posturing, making any attempt at standardized process control completely irrelevant.

The Burner Spreadsheets
I always start with good intentions. I build a master cloud spreadsheet with data validation for guest arrivals, room allocations, and transport mapping, treating the event like a large-scale project tracking non-value-added time. But because I can never get my extended family to actually input their PNR numbers, the digital infrastructure is abandoned by day two. The actual tracking system devolves into me frantically scribbling train timings and driver phone numbers on the back of Haldiram’s receipts stuffed into my kurta pocket.

WhatsApp Triangulation
The communication flow is an unscalable nightmare. There is the "Official Wedding" group (purely for forwarding invitation graphics and emojis) and the "Logistics" group (which is just people asking questions that were answered three scrolls up). The real system is me triangulating information by directly DMing three different cousins to figure out who is actually sitting in which car. It is a completely manual, point-to-point network that practically guarantees someone’s luggage will end up at the wrong guesthouse.

Dad: "Did you find the boot latch mechanism for the car? The mechanic says he needs it before 4 PM or the car stays overnight."
Me: "I've messaged 5 different spare part dealers in the local auto market. Two replied- yes, we'll get it but won't send pictures to confirm the exact model. I'm going to have to drive down there and physically roam around shop-to-shop to verify it. myself."

Why I'd hand it off:
Sourcing specific automotive spare parts locally is an absolute black hole for time. Standard quick-commerce apps don't stock highly specific mechanical components, and traditional e-commerce takes three days to deliver. When a mechanic needs a part today, you are forced into the offline, unstructured auto market. Last week, I wasted an entire afternoon roaming across half a dozen different shops in the heat, dealing with vague inventory claims, just to find a single matching boot strut.

Nobody has automated this because local spare part dealers do not maintain digitized, cloud-synced inventory systems. Their stock catalog lives entirely in their visual memory. Traditional software fails because you cannot scrape an API that doesn't exist. If I had a competent assistant, they would simply voice-call a designated network of local dealers, aggressively verify the exact part specifications over the phone, lock in the negotiated price via an instant digital payment, and dispatch a local logistics rider to pick it up. It takes a purely physical, frustrating wild-goose chase and turns it into a seamless digital transaction.

It is a completely opaque, offline market where inventory only exists in the shopkeeper's head.

It’s a massive pain every time because you are completely at their mercy. I finally found the part, paid via a direct WhatsApp UPI scan, and rushed back to the mechanic. One situation that really comes to mind was trying to sort out an investment and insurance decision at the same time. I was comparing different investment options, checking the returns, charges, lock-in periods, and trying to understand exactly what I was actually getting for the money. On top of that, I had to deal with different people explaining different things, and every answer seemed to lead to another question.

I remember spending a lot of time going through documents, checking numbers online, asking for clarification, and following up because the information I was getting was either incomplete or difficult to understand. I wasn't just trying to decide where to put my money—I had to figure out which option actually made sense for me, what the risks were, what fees I would be paying, and what would happen if I wanted to withdraw the money later. It became unnecessarily complicated for something that should have been a fairly straightforward decision.

The frustrating part was having to keep track of all the details myself and repeatedly chase people for clear answers. That was exactly the kind of task I would have happily handed over to a human assistant: compare the options, organize the information, point out the important differences, follow up with the right people, and give me a simple summary of what I actually needed to know.
column25:
My current system is a mix of personal tracking, apps, and occasional help from family or people who understand these things better than I do. I usually handle day-to-day money decisions myself, including keeping track of expenses, checking my bank accounts, managing payments, and deciding how much I want to save or invest. For investments, I generally use apps and online platforms to monitor my portfolio, check returns, compare options, and keep an eye on whether anything needs my attention.

For bigger financial decisions, especially investments or insurance, I usually don't rely on just one source. I might discuss it with a family member, look up information online, compare different plans, and sometimes speak to a broker or agent. WhatsApp and chats also end up being a surprisingly important part of the system because that's often where follow-ups, documents, recommendations, and reminders happen.

The system isn't particularly organized. Some information is in apps, some is in bank statements or emails, some is buried in WhatsApp conversations, and some is simply in my head. I don't have one central place where I can see everything—investments, insurance policies, upcoming payments, documents, and financial goals—in one view. So when something important comes up, I usually have to search through multiple places and piece everything together myself.

For most people, it’s not a single streamlined pipeline but a patchwork of overlapping habits:  

- Family coordination: One person casually mentions dates in a WhatsApp group, another checks school calendars, and suddenly the trip is half‑planned without anyone officially deciding.  
- Broker or agent: For bigger journeys, someone still calls “that uncle’s friend’s travel agent” who knows how to get tickets cheaper than any app. It feels old‑fashioned, but it works.  
- Apps and chats: Flights are booked on MakeMyTrip or Cleartrip, but hotels are discussed endlessly in group chats, with screenshots flying around. Half the time, the final booking is made by whoever loses patience first.  
- House staff reminders: In some households, staff quietly keep track of things like “don’t forget to stop the milk delivery” or “lock the balcony door,” which is as crucial as the tickets themselves.  
- Nothing at all: And then there’s the fallback system — no system. A bag is packed the night before, someone forgets chargers, and improvisation becomes the holiday theme.  

The roundabout part is that all these layers coexist. You might book flights on an app, confirm dates in a chat, rely on family to handle logistics, and still call an agent for “backup.” It’s messy, but it’s also what makes travel feel like a collective ritual rather than a transaction.

When it comes to money, investing, and insurance, I find it frustrating to choose the right option. There are so many insurance plans and investment products in the market, and every one of them has its own advantages and disadvantages. With insurance, I have to collect different quotations, compare coverage, exclusions, premiums, and benefits, and then make a decision. Having more choices gives us more opportunities, but it also creates more confusion and anxiety.

I experienced something similar when I was planning to invest in digital gold. My research suggested that gold prices were already high and could fall in the future, so I chose digital silver instead because the market trends showed strong growth. But later, silver prices started falling while gold continued to rise. It was frustrating to realize that even after spending so much time researching and studying investment strategies, the outcome could still be completely different.

The more choices we have, the more time and energy we spend trying to make the “right” decision and sometimes we still don't know whether it was the right one.

Seen.

Silence again.

My grandma was unwell and I was in Gurugram. He was in Telangana.

The doctor asked for his previous reports. They were scattered across
three places: a folder at home nobody could find, a WhatsApp forward
from six months ago buried under 3,000 messages, and one physical
paper that my mother was holding in her hand but could not read
because it was in English.

I spent 45 minutes on a call, directing my family to scroll, search,
and photograph documents while I tried to piece together his medical
history in real time.

The doctor waited.

We found most of it. Not all of it.

The frustrating part was not the distance. It was that every single
report existed somewhere. Nothing was lost. It was just scattered,
unreadable, and impossible to find fast when it actually mattered.
column19:
My system is my mother.

She remembers every doctor's name, every medicine, every follow-up
date, and every report that was ever generated in our family. She
carries it all in her head because there is nowhere else to put it.

When something happens, I call her first. She tells me which doctor
we saw last time, what he said, and which folder the reports might
be in. Then I call the doctor. Then I call my father to find the
folder. Then I call my mother again to translate what the report says.

The system works because she has never forgotten anything in 25 years.

It will break the day she is the one who is unwell.

That is the part that keeps me up at night. The entire medical memory
of our family lives in one person, with no backup, no index, and no
way to hand it off.

in my muscle memory.

The repetitive part is not the travel. The travel is always
different. It is the forty five minutes before every trip
where I am doing the exact same seven things in the exact
same order on the exact same apps, producing the exact same
screenshots in the exact same WhatsApp chat with myself.

Twenty eight times.

An agent could have done this for me twenty seven trips ago.
column28:
A WhatsApp chat with myself and my mother's anxiety.

Every trip I open a chat I named "Sri Trips" and screenshot
everything into it. Train confirmation. Bus backup. Hostel
address. Emergency contact in that city if I have one.
Google Maps link to the last mile.

Then I send my mother a voice note with the full itinerary
because she will not sleep until she knows where I am going,
how I am getting there, and who to call if I do not check in.

That voice note is my backup system. If something goes wrong
and my phone is dead, my mother knows the plan.

I have done this twenty eight times.

The chat with myself has 847 screenshots in it.
The voice notes to my mother are how I know I actually
committed to the trip.

It is a terrible system. It has never failed.
